why.say: Same file, same 08/05/2026 offer. On Track A, Keystone tendered. Here it doesn't. That's Track B, and it's where we live for the rest of the day. Keystone Mutual is sitting on the 14-Day Gap and it won't move. Now, remember the order of operations from Day 2: BI has to be exhausted before UM opens. So one carrier with a $10,000 limit is holding the entire $40,000 stack behind it. That little padlock on the slide is the whole problem. And here's your part in it. You're the engine room. Your job isn't to decide what happens next; it's to prove the impasse with dates and put a decision-ready record in front of Atty. Thorne.
why.ask: If one $10,000 carrier can freeze $40,000, what does that tell you about how carefully we have to document every date?

theory.say: Let's get our vocabulary straight, because an impasse isn't a feeling. It's a stall the record proves. It starts with the stall itself, the adjuster's delay line, something like "I'm waiting on authority." It's meant to wear you down. You log it; you never accept it. Every stall gets a rebuttal: a factual answer and a firm reply date. And a rebuttal that goes unanswered? That becomes evidence of impasse. Always ask the carrier to put its reasons in writing, because a named ground can be rebutted and a vague one can't. Finally, keep the four elements in your head: duty, breach, causation and damages. Any suit has to prove all four, so each one needs a verified exhibit behind it.
theory.ask: Which of these have you met before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: These are the three stalls you'll hear most, so let's practice answering them. First, "I'm waiting on my manager's authority." Fine. You set a firm reply date, and once it passes, the file goes to counsel. Second, "We need records from five years ago." Ask why they matter, and make clear you expect a good-faith offer on the undisputed injuries now, not after a fishing trip. Third, the classic: "The Property Damage was too low for this injury." Low-velocity impacts can still injure the spine, and you point them straight to the imaging. Notice the pattern. Every answer is calm, factual, and moves the clock forward.
frame.ask: Looking at John Doe's file, which of these stalls is Keystone using right now, and how did we answer it?

rules.say: Here's where Track B splits. Keystone holds at $3,500, calls it "final" on 08/12 and lets the demand lapse 08/21. We work the dispute path first, with evidence, new findings and the 09/02 supervisor escalation, and we document impasse on its triggers, not on frustration. By 09/04/2026 all five are on this file. Never bid against yourself. And know the cost: $40,000 frozen behind a $10,000 carrier, though exhaustion rules vary, so Atty. Thorne confirms. Filing is his decision; the inputs are yours: RPD-26-018842, Ruth Calloway, the doorbell video, the MRI, $16,450.19 in Specials, SOL 02/06/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027. Record the lapse, don't interpret it. You document and ask; you never recommend suit, value the claim, assess Robert Smith's exposure, or advise John Doe on the $3,500. A new number from Keystone goes to Atty. Thorne the same day.
rules.ask: Keystone hasn't said no. It has said nothing. When does silence become an impasse, and who decides that it has?

model.say: Take a look at this fork. On the left there's one trunk: same file, 08/05/2026, a $3,500 offer. The top branch, grayed out, is Track A from earlier today, the tender that opened UM. The bottom branch in orange is today. Follow the stations along it: 08/12 "final," the 08/21 lapse, the follow-ups on 08/24 and 08/31, the 09/02 escalation, and silence on 09/04. It ends at the impasse memo on 09/08, and Atty. Thorne decides. Now look underneath at the three rungs of the stack, $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000, with a red padlock on the BI rung. That's $40,000 frozen behind a $10,000 carrier. The padlock is the argument.
model.ask: Which station on that orange branch would you point to as the moment the record started to prove impasse?

job.say: Let me walk you through how this actually runs on a Tuesday. An offer gets repeated, or a demand deadline passes without acceptance. That's a trigger, so you log it in the CMS Communications Log with its date and its proof; every trigger dated and tied to a document. Then the follow-ups go unanswered. You escalate to the adjuster's supervisor through the Email Workspace, and you send no new number. That escalation asks for Keystone's written position and evidence, and it reopens no deadline unless Atty. Thorne approved the wording. When the escalation window closes in silence, you assemble the impasse record and the filing inputs, and route it to him through Tasks, Escalate, with the SOL and internal dates on it.
job.ask: When the supervisor escalation goes unanswered, why do we route the record to counsel instead of trying one more follow-up?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you call it Do or Don't, and then name the rule. This round's rules: date every contact the day it happens, ask the carrier for its reasons and evidence in writing, and escalate a silent adjuster to the supervisor before you call impasse. Watch for the traps too: waiting another month on a silent carrier, sending a UM demand before BI is exhausted, or telling John Doe the case "will have to go to court." That UM one is Day 2's order-of-operations error in new clothes. And if the 08/21 lapse might matter to Robert Smith's exposure, that's Atty. Thorne's analysis, never ours to write or say.
dodont.ask: Someone wants to just demand the UM limits while BI stalls. Do or Don't, and which rule decides it?

why.say: Look at that dashed pill that says PENDING. Here's my question: on 09/10/2026, what goes in the case-number field? Anything but "Pending" is a guess, and a guessed number ends up on a pleading. That's why this lesson matters. Once Atty. Thorne authorizes suit, a court clock replaces the adjuster's clock. Status, court fields, folders and calendar all have to change together. If they don't, you get a pre-lit file running on pre-lit habits while real court deadlines tick away. And later on, this file is going to meet two neutrals with very different power, so we'll start building that picture today too.
why.ask: On 09/10/2026, before anything is filed, what do you type in the case-number field?

theory.say: Filing the Complaint is what formally starts the lawsuit. From that moment the file moves out of negotiation and into court procedure, and later it'll meet a neutral the parties select or a court appoints. Counsel drafts the legal arguments in the Complaint; you verify the factual foundation underneath them. It has five sections you'll check against the file: caption, jurisdiction, factual allegations, causes of action and the prayer for relief. Before counsel signs, you confirm the Statute Date, the defendant's exact legal name, and for a business, its Registered Agent. And when we get to arbitration, AAA or JAMS sends a panel strike list. Each side vets, ranks and strikes names before a docketed cutoff.
theory.ask: Which of these pre-filing checks have you seen before, and where would John Doe's file need one?

frame.say: Let's open up a Complaint and go section by section. Up top is the caption: the court name, the parties and the official case number. Next comes jurisdiction, the legal basis for the court's authority to rule at all. Then the factual allegations, which is the story: the date, the location and the mechanics of the crash. Here's where your file work really shows, because every fact in there has to match what you've verified. After that, the causes of action, the legal claims, like negligence. And it closes with the prayer for relief, the explicit demand for remedies and money damages. Five sections, and you should be able to trace each one back to the file.
frame.ask: For John Doe, which of these five sections leans hardest on facts you personally verified?

rules.say: Status changes to Litigation only on Atty. Thorne's dated authorization, and it cites it. The fee follows the filing: 33⅓% pre-suit, 40% once suit is filed. Fill court fields only from the record; until filing, the number reads "Pending." Build the litigation directory at transition, DOE, JOHN - CASE FILE with folders 01 through 05, ready for the 09/24/2026 filing. Name every PDF properly, never scan001.pdf, and docket deadlines the day a document arrives. Seed the calendar: SOL 02/06/2028, hard date 02/04/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027, 48-hour audits. Notify the UM carriers in writing as Atty. Thorne directs, with no figure. Preserve the doorbell video unaltered and request preservation of what others hold. A binding award generally can't be appealed. You run fields, folders and logistics; what anything means for John Doe is Atty. Thorne's to explain, and at a hearing you never speak for him.
rules.ask: Which moves John Doe to the 40% tier: the status change or the filing?

model.say: This is a before-and-after. On the left, in muted gray, is the pre-lit file: a claim folder, an adjuster-response clock and a 33⅓% chip. A thick orange arrow crosses the middle, and it's labeled status to litigation, on counsel's authority. On the right, crisp navy, is the litigation and ADR file: a directory tree with the five numbered sub-folders, a court-fields card where the civil action number is still a dashed Pending pill, a calendar strip with a 48-hour audit flag before each hard date, and a 40% chip that says on filing. Underneath are the two neutrals: the mediator, with no power to decide, and the arbitrator, binding, with a red final seal.
model.ask: What's the single biggest difference between those two neutral cards at the bottom?

job.say: So how does this play out at your desk? Atty. Thorne authorizes suit, and that's your trigger. You change the status and open the court fields in Case Summary and Litigation, citing his dated authorization, with the case number still "Pending." Once status changes, you build the master directory and all five sub-folders under Documents, named exactly to the standard. With folders built, you seed the Litigation Calendar, making sure the SOL, the internal hard date, the cutoff and the 48-hour audits are all there. Later, when a panel list or a proposed neutral arrives, you pull resumes and prior-award history for Atty. Thorne and docket any strike deadline the same day. The strikes themselves are his call.
job.ask: A panel strike list lands on your desk. What do you do before the end of that day?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues go up one at a time; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. Here's what's in play: change status, fields, folders and calendar in one sitting; audit, don't just track; tailor the binder to the neutral, valuation for a mediator, evidence for an arbitrator; and leave expectations to Atty. Thorne. Traps include scan001.pdf in a litigation folder, treating mediation and arbitration as the same thing, missing a strike deadline, and assuming an arbitration error can be appealed. On that last one, there's no appeal on the merits, only a narrow motion for an evident miscalculation, on a short deadline. Prep has to be right the first time, because the rest of the litigation fork runs on what you build here.
dodont.ask: Can Atty. Thorne appeal an arbitration award that came in short because of a math error?

case.say: Here's what just landed on the file, dated 09/08/2026. It's from Atty. Thorne: "Got your 09/04 escalation task. Keystone has said nothing since the 09/02 supervisor escalation. Before I decide anything, send me the full impasse memo today." Here's the background. Keystone, Dana Whitfield on claim KM-26-440871, offered $3,500 on 08/05, citing the 14-Day Gap and a "degenerative" MRI. Our 08/06 rebuttal sent Dr. Helen Park's read, Dr. Reyes's 06/19/2026 Causation Letter, the EMS report and the Gap Explanation Record. On 08/12 Keystone called $3,500 "final." The demand lapsed 08/21. Follow-ups on 08/24 and 08/31 got nothing, and so did the 09/02 escalation. Before you write a single sentence, build your chronology. The dates are the memo.
case.ask: Before you draft anything, which event on this chronology are you least sure you can prove?

task.say: You're drafting the impasse memo to Atty. Elijah Thorne in the Action Plan Editor, pulling proof from the Communications Log and routing it through Tasks, Escalate. Start with a dated chronology from the 07/20/2026 demand through 09/04, every event tied to its proof. State Keystone's grounds and the rebuttal evidence it never answered. Show the frozen stack layer by layer, $30,000 of the $40,000 locked behind BI, with the documented Specials. Then the clock: SOL 02/06/2028, hard date 02/04/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027. End with the decisions you need from him, framed as questions. That's the graded judgment here. The memo documents and asks; it recommends nothing, because filing is his call.
task.ask: What is the one thing this memo must not contain?

check.say: Before you log this, check it hard. Your chronology runs 07/20 through 09/04 in order, and every event has a receipt, sent email or log entry behind it. An attempt with no proof is an assertion, not a record. Quote Keystone's grounds as Keystone gave them, and list the unanswered rebuttal. Show the whole stack: $10,000 BI unexhausted, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM closed. If your memo says "$10,000 available, UM pending," fix it. Specials are $14,817.40 plus $1,584.00 plus $48.79, so $16,450.19. Clock dates are right, routed Tuesday 09/08 after Labor Day. Your decisions are questions, with no recommendation and no new number to Keystone. Could he decide from it in five minutes?
check.ask: Does any sentence in your memo read like advice instead of a question for Atty. Thorne?

case.say: This one landed on 09/10/2026, from Atty. Thorne: "Yesterday I authorized suit against Robert Smith in the State Court of Riverton County, filing target 09/24/2026, and went over the fee tier with John. Transition the file today." He wants impasse notices drafted to Harbor Point, that's Marcus Bell on HP-26-7741, and to Cardinal State, Teresa Okafor on CS-26-20355, plus preservation requests for the doorbell video and the Escape's data recorder, all for his signature. Keep in mind Harbor Point's UM policy has an arbitration clause, the video copy was secured 02/19/2026, and the 2020 Ford Escape is Kevin Alvarez's. We'll run this as a live CMS session, and as you make each change, I want to hear the authority behind it out loud.
case.ask: When you change the status, what exactly will you say is the authority behind it?

task.say: You're working live in the CMS: Case Summary, Litigation, Documents, Outgoing, and the Calendar. Set the status on the 09/09 authorization. Open the court fields without guessing a case number. Record the fee tier exactly as the retainer sets it. Build the five litigation folders to firm standard. Draft both UM notices and the preservation requests for the doorbell video and the Escape's event data recorder, all for his approval. Open the ADR fields and seed the Litigation Calendar with 48-hour audits. When you're done, you hand in a file in Litigation status where every field, folder, notice, preservation step and date rests on Atty. Thorne's authority. The graded part is what those notices may and may not say.
task.ask: Marcus Bell calls after reading your notice and asks what you're demanding. What do you say?

check.say: Run down your work before you log it. Status is Litigation dated 09/10/2026, citing the 09/09 authorization. The court is the State Court of Riverton County, case number "Pending, assigned on filing." Fee tier: 40% from the filing date, not 09/10, and you note his discussion with John Doe without explaining it. Five folders, named exactly. Both notices state impasse and intended suit, carry their own claim number, have no figure, and go for approval. Now preservation, the step people skip because the video was secured in February. Request that Margaret Doe keep what she still holds, and draft the data recorder request to Kevin Alvarez and Harbor Point. Flag the arbitration clause and UM deadlines as questions. Calendar: 09/24 filing, 09/22 audit, plus the SOL dates.
check.ask: What does Margaret Doe still hold today, and who holds the Escape's event data recorder?

questions.say: Okay, time for the Learning Check. Answer each question from this file, in your own words, and type your answer right under the question. Start with question 1, because it's the foundation: explain the fork, what's the same on Track B as on Track A, what changes on 08/12/2026, and why a $10,000 carrier freezes all $40,000. If you can't explain that last part in plain words, flag me, and we'll revisit Day 2's order of operations together before moving on.
questions.ask: Can you explain, in one sentence, why $10,000 freezes $40,000?

summary.say: Next is your Self-Summary. Put the principles in your own words, not mine. Then work the scenario. It's 09/04/2026, Keystone has ignored two follow-ups and the 48-hour escalation, and John Doe calls asking why nothing's happening and whether he should just take the $3,500. Tell me what you say, what you don't say, and what goes to Atty. Thorne today. The strong answer takes the question down, tells John it's going to Atty. Thorne today, and gives no view on the $3,500 and no explanation of the fee.
summary.ask: When John asks if he should take the $3,500, what are the first words out of your mouth?

scale.say: Last step: the Skill Scale. Rate yourself on each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, and then submit it for review. I'll be comparing your self-rating against your score, and if there's a wide gap either way, we'll talk it through. One thing to remember, though: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach.
scale.ask: Where do you expect your self-rating and your score to disagree most?

why.say: I'm writing a date on the board: 02/06/2028. That's John Doe's statute of limitations. Quick, what day of the week is it? It's a Sunday, and that matters more than you'd think. Here's the bigger picture. Keystone's stonewall on the 14-Day Gap pushed this file onto court time. From 09/24/2026 on, its dates are set by rule, order and statute, and they don't move because a carrier goes quiet or a client can't be reached. One miscounted day can concede a fact or end a claim. That's why you'll see two orange pins stepping back from that Sunday. Those are the dates we actually live by.
why.ask: What day of the week is 02/06/2028, and why should that make us nervous?

theory.say: Once suit is filed, the whole game changes. Statute, rule and order set the dates, and your documents stop being administrative tracking and start being evidence. A missing or misfiled page isn't a clerical slip anymore; it can jeopardize a trial. Litigation runs on recurring court processes you'll execute every single week, each one driven by the calendar. Lots of steps carry a built-in wait, like the notice to opposing counsel before a third-party subpoena, and you docket that wait just like a deadline. And even when the deadline belongs to someone else, say a records office, you still check in days ahead. Their miss becomes your problem.
theory.ask: Which of these court habits will feel most different from how you ran the file pre-suit?

frame.say: Let's walk a subpoena from start to finish, because it shows how waiting periods work. You start by drafting the court-approved Subpoena Duces Tecum, which is a command to produce documents. Before it goes anywhere, you serve the defense a copy. Most states require 5 to 10 days' notice to opposing counsel, and that wait goes on your calendar. Then comes formal service, where a process server delivers it to the facility's Registered Agent. And finally, you track compliance. Five days before the deadline, you call the facility's legal or records department. Don't wait to discover on the due date that nothing's coming.
frame.ask: If John Doe's file needed records from a new provider today, which step would you be on first?

rules.say: A hard rule is a date fixed by statute, court rule, order or a forum's rules; miss one and the claim can go. Every date here is configured for this training file, and Atty. Thorne confirms the real rule. Exclude the trigger day, include the last: Robert Smith was served 10/14/2026, so his answer was due 11/13/2026. Watch the mailbox trap: this file's rules add 3 days for mail, though e-service adds nothing. Forward counts roll to the next business day; backward counts roll earlier. RFAs get their own entry, since unanswered ones may be deemed admitted. The Sunday SOL becomes an internal hard date of 02/04/2028 and a cutoff of 11/05/2027, both live until he releases them. Read every verb in the Scheduling Order. When unsure, docket the conservative date and flag it. You compute and docket; you never pick the rule or agree an extension.
rules.ask: Discovery was mailed to us on 12/01/2026. Walk me through every step: when are John Doe's responses due?

model.say: Here's this file's master calendar, laid out as one ribbon from 10/2026 to 02/2028. Above it, in navy, are the court's hard rules: 11/13/2026, 01/04/2027, 03/31/2027 and 05/28/2027. Hanging below, in orange, are the forum dates: 03/11, 03/18, 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027. Way out on the right there's a red flag on 02/06/2028 that says it's a Sunday, never rely on it, and two orange pins stepping back: the 02/04/2028 internal hard date and the 11/05/2027 filing cutoff. Underneath are two chips pointing opposite ways, forward counts go to the next business day, backward counts to the earlier one. Notice the pattern: what we docket always sits earlier than what the law allows.
model.ask: Why do you think the firm insists the dates we docket sit earlier than the law requires?

job.say: Picture the week of 12/10/2026. The Scheduling Order gets entered, and that same day you enter every date in the Docket System with its trigger, rule, owner and alerts, reading each verb, so "completed by" goes in as a deadline. The discovery that came by mail on 12/01/2026? You count 30 plus 3, see it lands on a Sunday, move it forward, and enter the RFAs separately in the Conflict Resolver, so responses and RFAs both sit at 01/04/2027 with the deemed-admitted flag set. On SOL review, 02/04/2028 and 11/05/2027 go on the CMS Calendar, and nothing relies on 02/06/2028. Then when arbitration is invoked on 04/05/2027, you hard-code 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027 with alerts the same day.
job.ask: Why do the RFAs get their own entry instead of riding along with the rest of the discovery?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you shout Do or Don't, then name the rule behind it. The rules in play this time: record the trigger, the rule and the arithmetic on every entry so anyone can re-check it, add warning alerts ahead of each hard date, and calendar the conservative date when a rule's unclear, then flag it. The traps: counting the trigger day as day one, rolling a backward-counted deadline forward to Monday, and docketing the SOL on its Sunday and trusting the roll-forward. Direction is the one people miss most. Roll the 06/12/2027 brief to Monday and it's filed late. And remember, you compute and docket; you never agree an extension.
dodont.ask: The brief's backward count lands on Saturday 06/12/2027. Do you move it to Monday, and which rule says so?

why.say: Before we talk procedure, one question. Whose insurance company are we fighting? Keystone insured Robert Smith, the man who ran the stop sign, so that claim is against somebody else's carrier. Harbor Point and Cardinal State are different. They are John's own coverage, under contracts he can call on, and that changes what this file is. When Harbor Point came back with eight thousand dollars against a twenty thousand dollar limit, we did not simply head for court the way the bodily injury claim would have. Harbor Point's own policy says where a dispute under it is decided, and reading that clause is our job before a single date goes on the calendar.
why.ask: What changes about a claim when the insurance company on the other end of it is our own client's?

theory.say: Let's name the two shapes. A third-party claim is made against the at-fault driver's carrier: Keystone, for Robert Smith. A first-party claim is made against your own insurance, on the policy you pay the premiums for. Here that is Harbor Point for Host UM and Cardinal State for Relative UM. Plain English for the client: one is a claim against the other driver's insurance, the other is a claim against your own. Then there is the mandatory arbitration clause, a policy term that sends the dispute to an arbitrator, so the firm files a Demand for Arbitration instead of a complaint. And off to one side, insurance bad faith: a separate suit about unreasonable handling, which can reach above the policy limit.
theory.ask: Why would a carrier rather have a UM dispute heard by an arbitrator than by a jury?

frame.say: Three steps, and I want you to see the third one as a fork. Step one, claim submission: the UM Demand Package goes out with proof that the at-fault limits were exhausted. On this file that went to Harbor Point and Cardinal State on the thirty-first of August. Step two, dispute: the carrier offers far under value, or denies liability or coverage. Eight thousand from Harbor Point, six thousand from Cardinal State. Step three, the resolution route, and here the road splits: a Demand for Arbitration where the policy's clause binds, or a civil suit against the carrier where the state's law bars that clause or lets the insured opt out. Bad faith is not on this flow at all. It is a separate action about handling, and it is Atty. Thorne's call alone.
frame.ask: Which of those three steps is the one where a Case Manager can do real damage by guessing?

rules.say: Start by knowing which claim you are on, because the evidence is the same but the relationship is not. Next, John's own Bluewater policy is not a UM layer at all: he rejected UM in writing in March of twenty twenty-four. He reaches UM by status instead, as an occupant of Kevin Alvarez's Escape and as a resident relative of his mother, Margaret. Third, and say this one back to me later: the route is read, never chosen. State law and the clause in the policy the claim is made under decide it. Fourth, read each layer on its own. Harbor Point's clause does not speak for Cardinal State. And every route carries its own clock, which is not the tort statute of limitations in February of twenty twenty-eight. Ask Atty. Thorne in writing, and docket only from his answer.
rules.ask: If Harbor Point's policy has an arbitration clause, what do we know about Cardinal State's?

model.say: Look at the flow on the file as it actually ran. Claim submission, the thirty-first of August twenty twenty-six: the demands carried the injuries, the records, sixteen thousand four hundred and fifty dollars nineteen in Specials, the wage letter, and the documented proof that Keystone's ten thousand was tendered and consented to. Dispute: eight thousand on the fourteenth of September, six thousand on the first of October, fourteen thousand offered against thirty thousand of limits. Resolution route: Harbor Point invoked its arbitration clause, it was taken up in April twenty twenty-seven, and the hearing ran on the twenty-second of June before Laura Whitcomb. And notice the last row of that table. John's Bluewater policy is not a route, because the coverage was rejected in writing.
model.ask: Which document on this file proves step one was complete before step two could even be argued?

job.say: On the job this is four triggers. When the UM offers come back low, you write the impasse memo the same day and you pull both carriers' dispute-resolution clauses from the certified policies, quoted and not interpreted. When the clauses and the statute are in hand, you lay the route options before Atty. Thorne as findings, with each layer's own filing or demand deadline put to him as a question. When he decides in writing, you record it: the ADR entry typed as UM slash UIM arbitration, how it was set as required by the policy or contract, and the case status matching the route. And when arbitration is invoked, you docket the hearing and everything counted back from it, and you tell John what happens procedurally and nothing more.
job.ask: Which of those four steps is the one trainees skip, and what does skipping it cost?

dodont.say: Two habits to keep. Say which kind of claim you are on before you say anything else about it, because first party or third party decides everything that follows. And quote the clause in your memo and then stop, because a paraphrase is already an interpretation and interpretation is not yours. Three to avoid. Do not file, or tell the client the firm is filing, a lawsuit when the policy sends that dispute to arbitration. Do not read Harbor Point's arbitration clause onto Cardinal State's policy just because both say UM on the front. And do not tell John the carrier is acting in bad faith or that he can recover above his limits, however much you want to.
dodont.ask: Why is the bad-faith line the most tempting one to cross on a file like this?

why.say: Two names, side by side: Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) and Laura Whitcomb, Esq. Tell me what each one can do to John Doe's case. Judge Benton is our mediator, and she can't decide anything. She can only help the parties agree, and any deal needs John's agreement, through Atty. Thorne. Laura Whitcomb is the arbitrator, and she decides. Her award stands with almost no appeal. These two sessions are three months apart, and here's the danger. If you prepare for both the same way, you'll walk a compromise file into a trial-ready hearing. That's the mistake this lesson is built to prevent.
why.ask: What can Hon. Carla Benton do to John Doe's case that Laura Whitcomb can't, and the other way around?

map.say: Before we name either neutral, look at where these sessions sit. Treatment ends, the demand goes out, the carrier evaluates it. If both sides want to avoid court costs, legal fees and a public record, they can mediate right there, before a single page is filed. Arbitration can come that early too, but only where the client signed a clause that sends the dispute out of court, like rideshare terms or a treatment consent. When negotiation fails, as it did with Keystone, the complaint is filed and the court's clock starts. Discovery runs, and many courts order mediation before they will give you a trial date. After that, the parties can agree to binding arbitration, or the case is tried. Both of John Doe's sessions sit on the filed side of that line.
map.ask: Does mediation happen before a lawsuit is filed or after it?

theory.say: Two words, and I want you saying them in plain language. Non-binding, which is mediation: both sides have to agree, so nobody is forced to settle and the parties keep control of the outcome. Binding, which is arbitration: the decision is final and enforced like a court order, and a court will only look at it on very narrow grounds. Then where each one sits. Before filing, mediation usually comes after treatment and the demand, and arbitration comes only where a signed clause compels it. After filing, mediation is often ordered during discovery, and arbitration happens when the parties agree to leave the court system. Those four cards are what you explain to John Doe. What either one does to his claim is Atty. Thorne's to tell him.
theory.ask: Say it to me as you would to John Doe: what does non-binding mean, and what does binding mean?

frame.say: Let's line the two up row by row. The mediator's role is facilitator and negotiator; the arbitrator is a private judge and finder of fact. On decision authority, the mediator has zero. She can't force a settlement, rule or order a payout. The arbitrator has total authority and issues a binding Arbitration Award. Control of the outcome stays with the parties at mediation, since they decide whether to sign, while the arbitrator decides liability and damages and can exclude evidence. Review afterward? Mediation needs none because there's no ruling; arbitration gets court review on narrow grounds only. And that sets your standard: compromise focus for one, trial-ready for the other.
frame.ask: On John Doe's file, which of these two columns is he heading into next, and how do you know?

rules.say: Mediation is facilitated compromise: non-binding and confidential under the governing rule. Court-ordered means John Doe must attend, not agree. Binding arbitration, like Harbor Point's clause, makes the arbitrator the judge, with narrow court review. Here, BI settled at mediation on 03/18/2027, and the UM carriers' dispute over the gap went to a decision. Know the limits: damages are reduced first by the $10,000 BI paid, Harbor Point pays above that up to $20,000, Cardinal State's $10,000 behind it, and how an award applies is Atty. Thorne's analysis. For mediation, collect 3 to 4 windows first, book a private room, check the interpreter, hold his 2-hour buffer. For arbitration, contact the arbitrator's office only as he directs, and confirm the retainer in writing. And the Golden Rule: you never argue, speak on the record or represent John Doe. Asked about a bill, you defer and hand him the document.
rules.ask: The mediation was court-ordered. Did John Doe have to settle?

model.say: Here are the two forums on John Doe's file, facing each other. On the left, the lighter card: mediation, 03/18/2027, Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.), tagged non-binding, confidential, facilitates. On the right, the heavier navy card: binding arbitration, 06/22/2027, Laura Whitcomb, Esq., tagged acts as judge, binding award, appeal limited, with its hard dates underneath, 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027. An orange arrow joins them, compromise to trial-ready. Across the bottom runs the red-bordered UPL bar. What you can do: observe, log directives, update the CMS. What you never do: argue, speak on the record, speak for John Doe, negotiate. That bar spans both cards on purpose. The line is the same at both tables.
model.ask: Why do you think that UPL bar runs under both cards instead of just the arbitration one?

job.say: Let's run the real sequence. The order requires mediation by 03/31/2027, so before you ever contact the mediator's office, you collect 3 to 4 windows from Atty. Thorne, John Doe and opposing counsel in the Calendaring Simulators, and you make sure the session lands inside 03/31/2027. Opposing counsel rejects every window? You log the pushback and escalate the same day for an attorney-to-attorney call. Later, the arbitrator's fee schedule and retainer request arrive. You confirm the schedule, route the retainer to accounting, send the internal invites, and get payment confirmed in writing before the hearing. And when a directive comes from the bench, you log it as given in Case Notes, calendar it and memo Atty. Thorne that same day.
job.ask: Opposing counsel says no to every window you offered. What's your very next move?

dodont.say: It's 3 Clues, 1 Rule time. Three clues come up, you call Do or Don't, then tell me the rule. This round covers: your hearing notes become Atty. Thorne's post-hearing roadmap; collect every party's windows before the neutral's office hears from you; and confirm the retainer payment in writing, because unpaid retainers delay hearings. Traps include a mediation-quality binder at an arbitration, helpfully answering the arbitrator directly, and logging bench directives the next day from memory. Logistics aren't clerical. The private room, the 2-hour buffer and the interpreter check are what let Atty. Thorne and John Doe think clearly. Here's the Golden Rule once more: violating UPL rules puts both the Case Manager and the firm at risk.
dodont.ask: The arbitrator turns to you and asks about a bill. Do or Don't answer, and what do you actually say?

case.say: It's 12/10/2026, and here's what landed from Atty. Thorne: "The Scheduling Order was entered today; it's attached with the discovery Mercer mailed us on 12/01. While you were out, the calendar was re-keyed from the paper file: nothing verified, no alerts. Audit every entry against the order, the discovery and the SOL, correct what's wrong, and send me the correction log." The case is No. 26-CV-04417. The discovery is 25 Interrogatories, 30 Requests for Production and 15 RFAs. The order sets plaintiff's expert disclosure 03/15/2027, defense 04/15/2027, mediation completed by 03/31/2027, discovery closing 05/28/2027, pretrial 08/12/2027, trial 09/13/2027. I'm handing you the staged calendar. Before you recompute anything, initial the entries you'd sign your name to.
case.ask: How many errors do you think are hiding on this calendar?

task.say: You'll audit John Doe's calendar in the Case Docket and Calendar Conflict Resolver, against the 12/10/2026 order, the discovery mailed 12/01/2026 and the 02/06/2028 SOL. Recompute every entry from its trigger document: trigger day out, 3 mail days in, forward counts to the next business day, backward to the earlier one. Correct the errors, add what's missing, leave correct entries alone. Each entry gets its trigger, rule, arithmetic, owner and alerts, mirrored to the CMS Calendar. Rank errors by risk, log corrections in Case Notes and route them to Atty. Thorne. Heads up: Jenna Price, Atty. Mercer's paralegal, will call. Agree to nothing, log her words verbatim, and route it today.
task.ask: 12/31/2026 is wrong and 11/08/2027 is wrong. Which one could cost John Doe his claim?

model.say: This is the staged calendar exactly as it was keyed: unverified, no alerts. Every row has its as-keyed date and a blank status chip on the right. You'll set each one to verified, corrected or added. At the bottom there's a single dashed add-entry row, and notice it doesn't tell you what's missing or how much. That's on purpose. Down the right edge is a risk gauge with two bands. The red band on top is costs rights, for dates that are later than they should be or missing entirely. The gray band below is costs time, for dates that are too early. You'll drag each error onto that gauge, and the red band sits on top for a reason: rights before time.
model.ask: Why does a missing entry belong in the red band rather than the gray one?

check.say: Here's what your audit should show before you log it. Responses corrected to Monday 01/04/2027, since 12/01 plus 30 plus 3 lands on Sunday 01/03. The RFA entry added, all 15 due 01/04/2027, flagged deemed admitted if unanswered. People fix what's on the screen and miss what isn't, and that's the nearest, most severe deadline here. Expert disclosures un-swapped. Mediation entered as completed by 03/31/2027. Internal hard date 02/04/2028 added. Filing cutoff corrected from 11/08/2027 to 11/05/2027, rolled earlier, never forward. Correct entries verified and left alone. Errors ranked, rights ahead of time. Many courts accept a Monday filing after a Sunday deadline, but the firm won't rely on it, and calling opposing counsel about an extension fails the authority row.
check.ask: Did you recompute each date from its trigger document, or from the entry you were checking?

case.say: Fast-forward to 04/05/2027. The 03/18/2027 mediation before Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) produced Keystone's $10,000 BI tender. BI is exhausted, the UM consents are in, and Robert Smith is dismissed. Now Atty. Thorne writes: "Harbor Point and Cardinal State dispute damages, citing the gap. Harbor Point has invoked its UM arbitration clause and Cardinal State joins: one binding arbitration before Laura Whitcomb, Esq., hearing 06/22/2027." He wants the rules matrix, the exhibit and brief dates docketed today, and a map of what you do at the hearing. As configured for this file, exhibits are exchanged 20 days before the hearing and the brief is due 10 days before. Before anyone opens the editor, let's build two columns on the board.
case.ask: What changes operationally when a file moves from mediation to arbitration?

task.say: In the Action Plan Editor, you'll build the ADR rules matrix with two columns, the 03/18/2027 mediation and the 06/22/2027 arbitration. The rows cover the neutral and her power, binding effect and appeal, confidentiality, the opposing parties, the limits in play, the preparation standard, your hard dates and the logistics. Today you'll also hard-code the arbitration dates on the CMS Calendar, counting back from the hearing, with alerts. Then map the UPL boundary for the hearing: what you do, what you never do, and the exact words you'd say if Laura Whitcomb, Esq. asks you about a bill. You'll hand in the matrix, the docketed dates and a one-page boundary map, all routed to Atty. Thorne.
task.ask: On 03/18/2027 the other side was Robert Smith. Who is it on 06/22/2027, and what are they disputing?

model.say: Here's your canvas. Two-thirds of the slide is the matrix: row labels down the left for neutral and power, binding and appeal, confidentiality, opposing parties, limits in play, standard, hard dates and logistics. There's a lighter mediation column and a solid navy arbitration column, and every cell is empty and outlined in orange, waiting for you. The right third is a bird's-eye view of the hearing table. Atty. Thorne's seat is at the table edge with a speech mark. Yours sits behind his, with a speech mark struck through in red, and an orange arrow that says hand him the document. That struck-through speech mark is the whole point of the slide.
model.ask: Which cell in this matrix do you expect to be hardest to fill in correctly, and why?

check.say: Check your matrix before you log it. Mediation: Hon. Carla Benton facilitates only, non-binding, held 03/18/2027 inside 03/31/2027. Arbitration: Laura Whitcomb acts as judge, binding award, narrow review, under Harbor Point's clause with Cardinal State joined. Opposing parties went from Robert Smith to the UM carriers, who are now the other side. Limits in play: $20,000 plus $10,000, so $30,000. Exhibits 06/02/2027. The brief is the trap: 10 days back is Saturday 06/12, so it moves to Friday 06/11, never Monday 06/14. Logistics and your UPL map are in. And your deferral: "I'm the Case Manager providing administrative assistance; Atty. Thorne will address that." If you audited the Riverton Spine & Rehab bill, you'll want to answer. Don't.
check.ask: Say your deferral line out loud once: what are the exact words you'll use at the hearing?

case.say: It is the second of October twenty twenty-six, and we are on Track B. The UM demands went out at the end of August, after Keystone tendered its ten thousand in bodily injury limits on the twelfth with both UM carriers' written consents and a Limited Release signed on the twenty-eighth. Now the answers are in. Marcus Bell at Harbor Point offers eight thousand against a twenty thousand dollar Host UM limit, and he is calling the fourteen-day gap a causation problem. Teresa Okafor at Cardinal State offers six thousand against ten thousand. Harbor Point's policy has a binding arbitration clause. Cardinal State's certified policy was requested and has not arrived.
case.ask: Fourteen thousand offered against thirty thousand of limits. What is our first move, and what is not?

task.say: Route the impasse. Write the memo to Atty. Thorne: the offers set against the limits, Harbor Point's stated reason, and each layer's dispute-resolution clause quoted word for word, with Cardinal State's marked as outstanding. Lay out both routes and what each would require operationally. Then ask him three things in writing: which route governs on each layer, each layer's own suit or arbitration-demand deadline, and whether the two should be heard together. Set the CMS up to carry his answer, with the ADR entry, the status, and a task per open question. Draft the calendar entries, but do not save them. Then write what you will say to John when he calls to ask what happens now.
task.ask: Why do we draft the calendar entries and hold them instead of simply docketing them today?

model.say: Here is what a memo that works looks like. It opens with the numbers: eight thousand against twenty, six thousand against ten, fourteen against thirty in all, with the dates on each. Then exhaustion, evidenced rather than asserted: Keystone's tender on the twelfth of August, the consents on the twenty-fourth and the twenty-sixth, the Limited Release signed on the twenty-eighth. Then a section per layer. Harbor Point's arbitration paragraph is pasted in whole and identified as binding, and nothing more is said about it. Cardinal State's section says plainly that the certified policy was requested and has not arrived, and there is a chase task against it. Then three numbered questions. That is a memo he can decide from without opening the file.
model.ask: What is missing from that memo on purpose, and why is leaving it out the right call?

check.say: Check your work against this. Both claims named as first-party claims, distinct from the Keystone claim that closed in August. The figures exact, with their dates. Exhaustion documented rather than assumed. Harbor Point's clause quoted and called binding, with no interpretation. Cardinal State treated as its own layer, its certified policy marked outstanding, with a chase task, and Harbor Point's clause never read onto it. Both routes laid out with their operational consequences. Bad faith raised only as a question, with the handling dates recorded as facts. Three written questions asked. Nothing docketed, and the tort statute of limitations not used as a UM deadline. And the explanation to John procedural only: what a Demand for Arbitration is, that a neutral decides rather than a jury, and that Atty. Thorne will go through what it means.
check.ask: Whose work would you rather hand to Atty. Thorne: the memo with an answer in it, or the one with three questions?

questions.say: Into the Learning Check, three questions, one for each part of this module. Question 1 is all the date arithmetic in one: the discovery mailed on the first of December, the Sunday statute of limitations, both weekend directions, and what happens to an unanswered Request for Admission. Show me the working, not just the dates. Question 2 is the UM side: the two routes out of an impasse, what decides which one governs, where a bad-faith action sits, and why John’s own Bluewater policy is not a route. Question 3 puts mediation and arbitration on the timeline and asks for non-binding and binding in the words you would use with him.
questions.ask: Which of those three would you least like Atty. Thorne to find wrong in your answer, and why?

summary.say: Now write your Self-Summary: the principles from this module in your own words. Then take the scenario on the slide. It's 09/04/2026, Keystone has ignored two follow-ups and the 48-hour escalation, and John Doe calls asking why nothing's happening and whether he should just take the $3,500. Write what you say, what you don't say, and what goes to Atty. Thorne today. While you're writing, think about one date on this file you'd always check twice.
summary.ask: Which single date on this file would you check twice, and why?

scale.say: To finish, fill in the Skill Scale. Rate each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, and submit it for review. I'll put your self-rating next to your score, and where there's a wide gap, we'll talk it through. Same as every day, UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an answer that speaks for John Doe at the hearing or tells him whether to take a number.
scale.ask: Which competency here are you least sure you could perform under pressure at a live hearing?

why.say: Let me start with a question. What happens if Atty. Thorne gets an unorganized file the morning of the mediation? Think about it for a second. He loses momentum. He looks unprepared in front of the mediator. And he may concede a point simply because he couldn't find the proof in time. Remember, Keystone's stonewall on the 14-Day Gap is the reason John Doe's file is in suit at all. At the 03/18/2027 mediation, Atty. Thorne will have minutes to answer that argument. So every record, every figure, every quote has to sit in a known place. A binder he has to hunt through costs momentum, and it can cost a concession.
why.ask: What happens if Atty. Thorne gets an unorganized file the morning of the mediation?

theory.say: Think of the Mediation Binder as the attorney's cheat sheet. It holds the case's most critical documents, compiled so counsel never fumbles during a fast-paced compromise session. It opens with the executive summary and administration, a one-page snapshot that sets the framework: the parties, the order, the schedule. That's the first thing Atty. Thorne sees. Next come the mediation briefs, both sides' arguments read side by side, so he can prepare rebuttals before anyone sits down. Then the core pleadings, the filed documents that define what this suit is actually about. Those first three sections set the stage, and we'll pick up the other three on the next slide.
theory.ask: Which of these first three sections have you already started building on John Doe's file without realizing it?

theory2.say: Picking up where we left off, the back half of the binder is where the case gets proved. Section four is key evidence and liability, the smoking guns: raw evidence of liability, from reports to video stills to highlighted deposition pages. Section five is damages, financials and experts. That's the section that justifies counsel's dollar figure, with the records, the bills, the wage proof and the expert reports. And section six, settlement history and drafts, closes it out. It's there so Atty. Thorne can finalize any deal that's reached before anyone leaves the room. If a deal comes together at four in the afternoon, you don't want to be drafting from scratch.
theory2.ask: Why do you think settlement drafts belong in the binder before the session even starts?

frame.say: Here's the six-section binder in its fixed order. Section one holds the snapshot sheet, the mediation order or agreement, and the session schedule. Section two, our confidential statement and the defense's brief, if they exchanged one. Section three, the operative complaint and the answer with its affirmative defenses. Section four, the Police Report, photos and video stills, and deposition summaries with the key pages highlighted. Section five, the medical chart and bills ledger, the wage-loss proof and the expert reports. And section six, the Negotiation Log of every demand and offer, plus a draft release. Same order, every time, so Atty. Thorne's hand goes to the right tab without thinking.
frame.ask: On John Doe's file, which of these six sections do you think will take the most work to get right?

rules.say: The binder is Atty. Thorne's and the mediator's road map, indexed so any document is found in five seconds. Six numbered sections, fixed order, each tab matching one master index in the CMS, the single source of truth. The binder prints from the index, never the reverse. Exhibit numbers belong to the proceeding, Bates numbers to the page. Section three holds only the 09/24/2026 complaint and 11/12/2026 answer, which pleads comparative negligence, causation and failure to mitigate. Section five's ledger ties to the certified invoices, with the duplicate removed, $6,290.00 down to $6,105.00, for $16,450.19 total. Section six fixes Keystone's $3,500 baseline and holds a draft Limited Release. You're the QA auditor: OCR-searchable, statement delivered by 03/11/2027, audited 48 hours out. Arguments, positions and every number are his, and you never discuss value with anyone.
rules.ask: Where do you find the mediator's fee split, and why can't you just assume it's 50/50?

model.say: Here's John Doe's binder, open and seen from above. Six navy divider tabs step down the right edge, each with its orange number and section name, and beside each one a card listing this file's documents: RPD-26-018842, the EDR, the 03/13/2026 MRI, the $16,450.19 in Specials. Across the top runs the master index, one source of truth, with columns for exhibit, Bates, source and status. See those thin orange lines? They run from the index rows down into the tabs. On the right there's a stopwatch reading five seconds, and a red warning that drafts and superseded pleadings never enter the binder. The lines only run one way, from index to binder, never back.
model.ask: If the printed binder and the CMS index disagree, which one wins?

job.say: Here's the flow once the mediation is set for 03/18/2027. You open the master index under Documents and seat each document in exactly one section, so every entry has its section, exhibit number, Bates range and source. Once the pleadings and evidence are indexed, you go to the Pleadings Log and check each defense pleaded in the answer against sections four and five. Every pleaded defense needs an answering exhibit, or a flag to Atty. Thorne. Then, with the binder assembled, you OCR it, bookmark it, QA it against the index and route it for approval. It has to be text-searchable, approved, and delivered by 03/11/2027.
job.ask: A pleaded defense has no answering exhibit in sections four or five. What do you do with it?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll show three clues, you call Do or Don't and name the rule. In play: start from the 07/20/2026 Demand Package, since most of sections four and five already exist there, and bookmark to the page Atty. Thorne will quote, not the cover. The traps: an unorganized file the morning of, a snapshot sheet with stale opposing-counsel contacts, and the confidential statement sent ten minutes early or to the wrong person. Remember, the product is the index, and when two copies disagree, the index decides. And Dr. Reyes's causation opinion may need disclosure by 03/15/2027. You flag it to Atty. Thorne now, and how it's disclosed is his call.
dodont.ask: You bookmark Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter to its cover page. Do or Don't, and what's the rule?

why.say: I'm holding up the Mediation Binder. This one persuaded. The next one is evidence. And I'm writing a date on the board: 06/02/2027. Everything in this lesson counts back from that exchange. Here's why it matters. On 04/05/2027, Harbor Point and Cardinal State picked up Keystone's gap argument, and Laura Whitcomb, Esq. is going to decide damages, bindingly. The Arbitration Binder is the record her award rests on. A page that's missing, illegible or not exchanged by 06/02/2027 may simply not count. No second chances.
why.ask: What's the difference between a binder that persuades and a binder that's evidence?

theory.say: The Arbitration Binder isn't a reference packet. It's a trial-ready evidentiary record, handed straight to a private judge who decides. Your role here is operational: timelines, scheduling and documents, run with rigid precision. The arbitration brief deadline is the absolute cutoff for claims, exhibit indexes and witness lists, and it goes to the arbitrator and opposing counsel. The arbitration submissions are the foundational paperwork that sets the ground rules for the whole proceeding, which is why they lead the binder. And here's the scary part: a missing page or a grayscale print can be excluded, and with a binding award, there's no second chance to fix it.
theory.ask: Which of these four ideas feels most different from how we built the Mediation Binder?

frame.say: Six tabs again, but with a different job. Tab one, arbitration submissions: the snapshot sheet, the final brief, the governing order or agreement and fee disclosures. Tab two, arbitration pleadings: the operative demand and each party's written position, with no superseded versions. Tab three, liability and biomechanics: the certified Police Report, diagrams, and photos and stills in color, never grayscale. Tab four, medical damages: the consolidated ledger, provider records and bills, imaging, the causation opinion. Tab five is the prior medical shield, prior injury records and work history paired with a medical opinion. And tab six is economic losses, wage-loss proof only.
frame.ask: Looking at John Doe's file, which tab is going to carry the gap fight that the carriers are pressing?

rules.say: A binding award rests on the exhibits, with very limited review, so apply each tab's QC rule as you sort. The threshold leads: UM opens only because BI is exhausted, so prove it with Keystone's $10,000 tender, the consents, the Limited Release and Robert Smith's dismissal, never the Mediation Statement. Authenticate everything with business-records certifications from each provider, Riverton Fire, Riverton PD and Northgate HR. Keep video native, with the 02/19/2026 chain of custody, and print stills in color. Even if the forum relaxes evidence rules, build to the strict standard; admitted isn't persuasive. Number exhibits C-1 onward and freeze the set once exchanged. Nothing crosses over from mediation, and the Lien Sheet stays in Atty. Thorne's set. He decides what's argued, exchanged or withheld. You never argue an exhibit.
rules.ask: Who can say the doorbell video is what we say it is?

model.say: Look at the two panels. On the left, small and grayed out, is the Mediation Binder, captioned persuades, non-binding. A heavy orange arrow says the gap dispute carries over. On the right, much bigger, are the six arbitration tabs, each with a card stating its QC rule. Over tab one sits a threshold chip: BI exhausted, $10,000 tendered 03/18/2027. Under the tabs runs an authentication rail: custodian certification, native file, chain of custody. Bottom right is a red warning, not exchanged by 06/02/2027 means it may not count, with a reminder to confirm the forum's rules. That size difference is the message. This record is the one that decides.
model.ask: Why does the BI exhaustion proof sit on top of tab one, ahead of everything else?

job.say: Here's how it unfolds. Arbitration's invoked on 04/05/2027, so you open the claimant exhibit index and put the 06/02/2027 exchange and the 06/11/2027 brief on the Docket System that day. As the provider records come in, you go through Medical Records Requests and ask each custodian for a business-records certification, one per provider, covering every date you're exhibiting. Custodians are slow, so don't wait. Once the exchange set is assembled, you route the set and every flagged item to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate. It has to be approved before 06/02/2027, with no privileged item anywhere in it.
job.ask: Why do we request certifications the same week the arbitration is invoked rather than once the binder's built?

dodont.say: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, arbitration edition. Clues come up one at a time; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. Rules in play: build to the strict evidence standard even where the forum relaxes it, keep native video and data untouched and work from copies, and request certifications the week arbitration is invoked. Traps: a grayscale print of a crash still, a draft brief or superseded complaint in the exchanged set, or the Confidential Mediation Statement carried over. Say it back to me: relaxed admission is not full weight, and the clause may relax nothing at all. And on privilege, you flag and Atty. Thorne decides, because an internal memo in an exchanged set can't be unsent.
dodont.ask: The forum relaxes the rules of evidence, so you skip the custodian certification. Do or Don't, and why?

case.say: It's 03/04/2027, and this just came from Atty. Thorne: "Mercer writes that Keystone will not put a real number on the table while our medical ledger is unverified. The draft binder carries Riverton at $6,290.00 and Crescent as an open balance. Rebuild it from the master index and audit it." The statement and binder go to Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) by 03/11/2027, routed to him first, for the 03/18/2027 mediation. John Doe was deposed 02/18/2027, and the certified transcript's in the file. Riverton Spine & Rehab's Final Itemized Ledger, requested 02/08/2027, followed up 02/22 and red-flagged 03/01, still hasn't arrived. Now, see those two red landmine chips? Who spotted them in the draft before I pointed?
case.ask: Who spotted those two landmines in the draft before I pointed them out, and what tipped you off?

task.say: You'll assemble the six-section Mediation Binder in the CMS, working from the master index and starting with the 07/20/2026 Demand Package. Seat each document in one section with its exhibit number and Bates range, and map every allegation in the 11/12/2026 answer to the exhibit that answers it. Then run the pre-mediation audit. Rebuild the ledger from the certified bills you have to $16,450.19, and cross-check each provider balance against what PIP and Peach State already paid. Add the Negotiation Log, a draft Limited Release and the UM consent requests. You'll hand in an indexed, searchable binder with an audited ledger, a lien summary and a short memo on both landmines, routed to Atty. Thorne.
task.ask: Atty. Mercer says the ledger is unverified. Is he wrong?

check.say: Before you log this, run your checks. Section one's snapshot has LSH-2026-MVA-770412, No. 26-CV-04417, Atty. Mercer's verified contacts, and the fee split read from the order. Section three, only the filed complaint and answer. Your defense map gets graded hard: five allegations, five answers, each with an exhibit number, so "see Medical Records" isn't a map. Landmine one: Riverton audited to 33 visits at $185.00, $6,105.00, duplicate removed, pending final verification, for $16,450.19. Landmine two: Crescent's $3,400.00 satisfied by Peach State's $1,860.00, with open liens of $7,965.00. Section six's log runs from the 07/20/2026 demand to suit. The release and consent requests are drafts, so leave every term to Atty. Thorne. Then swap binders with your partner and QA each other's index.
check.ask: When you swap with your partner, which exhibit number in their defense map will you check first?

audit.say: This is the index the Litigation Desk assembled on the second of March, and Atty. Mercer says Keystone won't put a real number on the table while the medical ledger is unverified. On this draft he's right. Section five was typed from the providers' original bills, so Riverton Spine and Rehab comes in at six thousand two hundred and ninety on thirty-four lines and the medical total reads fifteen thousand and two forty, against the fourteen thousand eight hundred and seventeen forty we served in July. Crescent shows as an open balance Peach State already paid. Call every section, and tell me what's missing as well as what's wrong. When you hand it in you'll see the binder as we delivered it on the eleventh of March.
audit.ask: Two medical totals for one file. Which one would you defend in that room?

case.say: Here's what landed on 05/17/2027: exhibit exchange in 16 days, and the Arbitration Binder isn't started. Zero of six tabs. The hard date is 06/02/2027, before Laura Whitcomb, Esq., on HP-26-7741 and CS-26-20355. Robert Smith was dismissed after Keystone tendered its $10,000 at the 03/18/2027 mediation, and the carriers are disputing damages over the gap. The unsorted folder holds a pre-filing draft of the Complaint, grayscale doorbell stills, the 09/08/2026 impasse memo, and a Lien Sheet listing Harbor Point PIP at $5,000.00 and Summit Imaging at $2,395.00. Crescent Pain & Spine's certified records, requested 05/05/2027, haven't come in. I'm putting four red traps on the board, then covering them before anyone sorts.
case.ask: Before I cover them, which of those four traps do you think you'd have missed on your own?

task.say: You'll sort that folder into the six-tab Arbitration Binder using the Exhibit index, Medical Records Requests and the Lien Tracker, applying each tab's QC rule as you go. Lead with the BI exhaustion record, number every exhibit C-1 onward with its Bates range, and log each record's authentication. Then defuse both landmines. Build tab five's prior medical shield against the 2021 low-back visits defense counsel pressed at the 02/18/2027 deposition and the "degenerative" MRI reading from 08/05/2026, and strip the Lien Sheet to what's owed. Flag anything privileged for Atty. Thorne. You'll also take a call from Lori Banks at Crescent: identify the blockers, get a firm delivery date in writing, and log it.
task.ask: Harbor Point is the other side now. Our attorney's-set Lien Sheet says it is owed $5,000.00. What goes wrong?

check.say: Check before you log. Tab one has the snapshot and the 06/11/2027 brief slot, never a draft. Threshold exhibits come first, the $10,000 tender, consents, Limited Release, dismissal and both Coverage Letters. Tab two holds operative versions only, with the pre-filing draft gone. Tab three has the certified RPD-26-018842 and color stills from the native file. Tab four ties $14,817.40 to certified bills, with certifications requested from each provider. On tab five, pull and pair the 2021 records with the MRI read and Causation Letter, but don't argue causation; a supplemental opinion from Dr. Reyes is Atty. Thorne's call. The Lien Sheet drops Harbor Point and Summit, leaving $7,965.00. Tab six is wages, $1,584.00. And the impasse memo is the privilege test. It never goes in tab six.
