audit.say: The desk's exhibit index, the fourteenth of May, and Harbor Point is on the other side of this hearing now. Decide for each exhibit which tab it belongs in, or that it's withheld, and apply the QC as you sort rather than after. The Confidential Mediation Statement is sitting at C-2 for background. Nobody has asked a single provider for a certification, the authentication log hasn't been started, and tab one has no exhaustion record at all, so there's nothing proving the bodily injury layer is gone. And the Lien Sheet claims five thousand dollars for Harbor Point MedPay, which gave up any reimbursement right in writing in March. When you hand it in you'll see the set we exchanged on the second of June.
audit.ask: Harbor Point is the opponent now. What changes about what we send?

questions.say: Time for the Learning Check, and I want you to put your two master indexes side by side before you start. This check is about the binders you actually built, not your memory of my slides. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed right under each question. You'll name the six mediation sections with a document for each, explain what the master index records and why it's the source of truth, and trace the unbelted defense to the exhibits that answer it.
questions.ask: Looking at your two indexes side by side, where do they differ most in how they're organized?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary: write the principles in your own words. Then take the scenario on the slide, John Doe on 09/04/2026 asking whether he should just take the $3,500, and write what you'd say, what you wouldn't, and what goes to Atty. Thorne. On question 7, the pressure scenario, the strong answer requests the missing records and a certification covering all 33 visits at once, tells Atty. Thorne that evening, and leaves the exchange to him. Never exchange a ledger its records don't support.
summary.ask: Which document would hurt John Doe most if it were missing from these binders, and which would hurt most if it were included?

scale.say: Last piece: the Skill Scale. Rate each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll put your rating next to your score, and if they're far apart, we'll talk about why. And remember, UPL is a gate here too. A strong score doesn't survive a privileged memo landing in an exchanged set.
scale.ask: Which binder skill would you rate yourself lowest on right now, and what would move it up a point?

why.say: Put two numbers side by side for me: $10,000 and $40,000. How much of John Doe's coverage did Keystone's silence lock? All of it. That's what one unmanaged bottleneck costs. On Track B, Keystone held at $3,500 on the 14-Day Gap, then went quiet, and a $10,000 carrier froze the whole $40,000 stack and forked the file into suit. Here's the tricky part. Bottlenecks rarely look dramatic. They look like a quiet inbox, a record that's "on its way," a date nobody's confirmed. Our job this module is to anticipate them and clear them before they cost us a deadline or an exhibit.
why.ask: How much of John Doe's coverage did Keystone's silence lock?

theory.say: Bottlenecks come in two families, and they hurt in different ways. Compromise traps stall a mediation: an unverified ledger, a representative with no authority, a late brief. Each one hands the defense a reason to stall. Trial-ready landmines are worse, because they sink a binding arbitration: excluded exhibits, unshielded priors, missed cutoffs. That's evidence you can't get back. One landmine deserves its own name, the prior medical shield. The defense will use prior records to argue a pre-existing degenerative condition, and the shield answers with records and expert opinion. The good news? Two habits clear most bottlenecks early: the 48-hour audit, and reconciling liens against the EOBs.
theory.ask: On John Doe's file, which of these bottleneck types have we already tripped over once?

frame.say: Here are the six bottlenecks you'll see most, three on each side. On the mediation side, there's the unverified ledger, where unreconciled bills or missing treatment logs make damages look unsupported. There's the missing decision-maker, a representative who shows up without full settlement authority. And there's the misaligned confidential brief, late or missing critical exhibits, which stalls the mediator's prep. On the arbitration side, there's evidentiary exclusion, missing documents or grayscale prints thrown out. There's the pre-existing defense trap, prior injury records left without an expert declaration. And calendar misses, whether unsynced windows for the neutral or a blown brief cutoff.
frame.ask: Pick one mediation bottleneck and one arbitration bottleneck. Where has John Doe's file faced each?

rules.say: A bottleneck is any dependency that can stop the file reaching a hard date. Log it the day it starts, with the date it threatens, and age it daily. Follow up a silent adjuster every 5 business days: Keystone left 08/24 and 08/31/2026 unanswered, then the 09/02 escalation. Silence is a position, so record it as dated facts, never "adjuster busy." A record unanswered after 14 days is a bottleneck, and the biggest mediation one is an unverified ledger: $16,450.19, Riverton at $6,105.00, Peach State at $1,860.00. Get verified ledgers to Keystone in time for an authority raise, the brief to Hon. Carla Benton by 03/11/2027, and stills printed in color. Shield the 2021 low-back visits as Atty. Thorne directs. Sync windows before offering dates. You chase, document and flag; legal remedies and value talk are his.
rules.ask: When did the Keystone bottleneck start: 08/21, 08/24 or 09/04?

model.say: Here's the Track B timeline across a navy rail, with the hard dates in pills: 08/21/2026, 03/11/2027, 03/18/2027, 03/31/2027, 06/02/2027 and 06/22/2027. Above it are three cards: non-responsive party, delayed record, and scheduling. Each one drops an orange line to the date it threatens. The non-responsive party card is the biggest, and underneath it there's a red callout: $10,000 carrier, $40,000 frozen. On the right edge are two chips. Mediation, where a gap costs leverage. Arbitration, where a gap costs evidence. Here's the takeaway: you measure a bottleneck by the hard date it threatens, not by how irritating it is.
model.ask: Why should the size of a bottleneck be measured by the date it threatens rather than how annoying it feels?

job.say: Let's run it like a real week. A follow-up goes unanswered, so you log it in the Communications Log with date, time, method and outcome, and you date the next follow-up five business days out. When the second one goes unanswered, you open an entry in the Bottleneck Log with the blocker, the start date and the hard date it threatens. For Keystone, the start date is the first unanswered request, 08/24/2026. When a proposed ADR date comes in, you run it through the Conflict Resolver against every party's window, so no mediation date after 03/31/2027 ever reaches Atty. Thorne as available. And when a binder dependency is still open 10 days out, you red-flag it, like the 03/01/2027 flag for the 03/11/2027 binder.
job.ask: Why does the bottleneck's start date go back to the first unanswered request instead of the day it started hurting?

dodont.say: Here comes 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, one at a time; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. This round: anticipate and eliminate, because a bottleneck found at the deadline was found too late; the single biggest mediation bottleneck is an unverified ledger; and follow up in writing as well as by phone, because a call alone proves nothing. Traps: a confidential statement reaching the mediator ten minutes before the session, grayscale stills for a binding hearing, and logging silence as "adjuster busy." Don't treat mediation and arbitration gaps alike. One costs leverage; the other can get evidence excluded. And remember, Keystone tendered $10,000 at mediation on 03/18/2027 because someone in that room could pay it.
dodont.ask: Keystone's adjuster arrives at mediation with authority well below the limits. What failed earlier, and which rule would have caught it?

why.say: Here's an escalation I see far too often: "Keystone still not responding, please advise." Look at that and tell me what Atty. Thorne has to go look up before he can do anything with it. When was the last contact? What deadline is at risk? What's been tried? What does he need to decide? Every one of your answers is a field that report should have carried. An escalation without the dates, the threatened deadline and a clear ask makes him do your research before he can decide. The ladder decides who hears about a bottleneck and when. The report decides whether they can act on it in one read.
why.ask: What does Atty. Thorne have to look up before he can act on "Keystone still not responding, please advise"?

theory.say: Think of escalation as a variance loop. You monitor each item against its expected course, and when progress stalls, you route it up before the date is lost. The trigger is the variance itself, the moment something departs from its expected course. Not frustration, not a hunch. Then the escalation ladder sends each problem to the lowest rung that can actually fix it, so counsel's time goes to decisions only he can make. What you send up is a decision-ready report, built so the supervisor can act in one read without redoing your work. And before every hard date, you run a critical thinking audit, testing the file against the defense's stated position and escalating any gap.
theory.ask: Can you think of a time a problem reached the boss before anyone at a lower level had a chance to fix it?

frame.say: This is the three-step protocol, and it's simpler than it sounds. Level one is the source. You follow up with whoever owes the item, on the cadence, and log the date, method and result every time. Level two is the Notice of Delay. That's written notice to the supervisor or office manager stating what's outstanding, since when, and the hard date it threatens. Level three is Atty. Thorne. You send him the five-field report, and if a motion to compel or a subpoena is on the table, that choice is his. Three rungs, in order, documented the whole way up.
frame.ask: With Riverton Spine & Rehab's overdue ledger, which rung would you be on by 02/22/2027?

rules.say: Climb one rung at a time and log each attempt: the source, then its supervisor with a written Notice of Delay, then Atty. Thorne. That notice states facts only and never argues bad faith or exposure. The 48-Hour Mandate times the climb. For Keystone, the second follow-up was 08/31, the supervisor got it 09/02, silence on 09/04 sent it to Atty. Thorne, and the impasse memo followed 09/08/2026. It also audits ledgers, binders and OCR 48 hours before every hard date. Rung three is where the legal tools live; you can name one as a question, but he decides, signs and sends. Don't skip, don't sit. Every report carries five fields: blocker, start date, hard date, what was tried, and the ask. Zero defaults: by the hard date, file what you have marked pending, or he holds a docketed extension. Report up weekly, never out.
rules.ask: Who should have heard about the Keystone silence first: Dana Whitfield's supervisor or Atty. Thorne?

model.say: On the left, there's a three-rung ladder, drawn bottom-up. Rung one is the source, rung two is the supervisor with a Notice of Delay, and rung three is Atty. Thorne, with a 48-hour pill between each pair. Under it, a red strip: don't skip, don't sit. On the right is the bottleneck report itself, filled in for Keystone exactly as it reached Atty. Thorne on 09/08/2026. Five fields, each with an orange badge: the blocker, when it started, what it threatens, what was tried, and the ask. The ask is boxed in orange and it's the only thing in bold. That's the point. Escalation is a sequence, and the report is what lets counsel act in one read.
model.ask: Why do you think the ask is the only field in bold on that report?

job.say: Here's the rhythm on the job. When rung one goes unanswered on its cadence, you send a written Notice of Delay to the supervisor or office manager from the Email Workspace, naming the item, its start date and the hard date, and you log it. If rung two sits unanswered for 48 hours, you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, with all five fields complete and one ask per blocker. Every week, on reporting day, you send him the Bottleneck Log, each item with its age and days to its hard date. And if a hard date arrives with the blocker still open, you prepare the filing with what you have, marked pending, or you confirm his extension is docketed. Zero defaults.
job.ask: A hard date arrives and one record is still missing. What are your only two acceptable options?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. The rules this round: climb one rung at a time and document each attempt, lead the report with the nearest hard date, and write the ask as one decision with the date it's needed by. Traps: going straight to Atty. Thorne before the source and supervisor have been tried, "Keystone still isn't responding, please advise" with no dates, and letting a deadline pass because a record was late. That last one's where people slip under pressure. Send what you have, marked pending, or have his extension docketed. Never neither. And subpoenas or motions to compel? You can name them; he decides.
dodont.ask: You hold the whole exhibit exchange to wait for one late record. Do or Don't, and which rule does it break?

case.say: This landed on 02/22/2027: record overdue 14 days, Riverton Spine & Rehab's Final Ledger. It was requested 02/08/2027 and still isn't here, and it's a dependency for the Mediation Binder due to Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) on 03/11/2027, ahead of the 03/18/2027 session. Keystone's attendee and their authority are unconfirmed, and there are no countermeasure rules on this file yet. The demand-stage audit holds Riverton at $6,105.00, 33 visits at $185.00, and Peach State's EOB shows $1,860.00 paid on Crescent's $3,400.00 bill. Before we touch the live dates, we'll calibrate. Let's enter the Keystone dates together and watch Rule 1 fire on 09/02 and 09/04. If a rule can't reproduce a known record, we can't trust it on a live one.
case.ask: If Rule 1 doesn't fire on 09/02 and 09/04 during calibration, what would that tell you?

task.say: You'll configure four countermeasure rules in the CMS under Tasks, Countermeasure rules, with the Calendar and Risk Flags. Rule one handles silence: follow-ups every 5 business days, then 48 hours after the second unanswered one it goes to the supervisor, and 48 more to Atty. Thorne. Rule two: a record not received 14 days after request gets a second request and a subpoena flag for him. Rule three: a hard date 10 days out with an open dependency gets a red flag. Rule four is the 48-Hour Mandate audit before every hard date, with its contents and a fallback. Calibrate rule one on Keystone, then fire all four on the mediation calendar with a date, action and owner each.
task.ask: The ledger is still missing at the 03/09/2027 audit. Do you hold the binder?

check.say: Let's check your dates, because every firing date is arithmetic from the file. Calibration fires 09/02/2026 and 09/04/2026, with the memo following 09/08. Rule two fires 02/22/2027, 02/08 plus 14, with a second request that day. Your subpoena flag should read as a question for Atty. Thorne, never as if it's decided. Rule three flags 03/01/2027 for the ledger and 03/08/2027 for Keystone's attendee with authority, the one people forget. Rule four audits 03/09 and 03/16/2027. Peach State's $1,860.00 closes Crescent's bill, so the $1,540.00 written off is never a lien. Your fallback includes the $6,105.00 interim ledger. Every firing has a date, action and owner, and no rule messages anyone outside on its own.
check.ask: Which of your firing dates would you double-check first, and why that one?

case.say: It's Monday, 05/24/2027, nine days to the 06/02/2027 exhibit exchange before Laura Whitcomb, Esq. Five open items. One, Crescent Pain & Spine's certified records for the 05/15/2026 injection: requested 05/05, second request 05/19, nothing yet. Two, Dr. Reyes's declaration shielding the 2021 low-back visits, and Lakeside says she's away until 06/01/2027. Three, Cardinal State's Teresa Okafor hasn't confirmed the hearing format or exchange method, and the 05/21 supervisor escalation is unanswered. Four, Riverton's refreshed ledger shows $6,290.00, the old duplicate restored. Five, the copy set prints the doorbell stills in grayscale with no OCR. Show of hands: which do you tackle first? Most people pick the grayscale reprint because it's easy. Easy isn't first.

task.say: You'll triage all five in the CMS, using the Conflict Resolver, the Bottleneck Log and Tasks, Escalate. For each one, name the hard date it threatens, the rung it's reached and the countermeasure that applies. Then put them in order: what goes to Atty. Thorne first, what you fix yourself today, and what the 48-hour audit verifies and when. You'll hand in one bottleneck report, sent 05/24/2027, carrying every item that needs his decision, five fields and one ask each. And there's a live call with Teresa Okafor. Ask whether Cardinal State has counsel, get format and exchange method confirmed in writing, and decline any talk of the gap or value.
task.ask: Which of these can still hurt John Doe after 06/22/2027?

check.say: Check your triage before you log it. Every item maps to the 06/02/2027 exchange, inside the red-flag window. Items one, two and three go to Atty. Thorne first, in one report on 05/24/2027, because each needs his decision. On item three, check CMS Parties for counsel first, and never email the arbitrator. That goes through Atty. Thorne. Its 48 hours ran out on a Sunday, so it's at rung three today. Item four you fix yourself: the set keeps $6,105.00 with the duplicate documented, because $6,290.00 invites the carriers to doubt every number, and Riverton's ledger also records the 19-day disruption. Item five, reprint in color and OCR. The audit lands Friday 05/28/2027, ahead of Memorial Day. And item one's root cause was our own late request.

questions.say: Let's wrap the module with the Learning Check. Answer from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. You'll name the three bottleneck families with this file's examples, walk Rule 1 on the Keystone record with every date, and explain what failed if Keystone's representative shows up without authority. Question 5 is the pressure scenario, and it's really the whole module in one question. If you'd hold the binder there, you've failed the 48-Hour Mandate.
questions.ask: In question 5, what are the four things you do when the ledger still hasn't arrived?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, the principles in your own words, plus the scenario on the slide. Before you write, think about question 7: Teresa Okafor calls. The compliant answer takes the message, says Atty. Thorne will respond, and logs it, without touching the gap argument or the offer. And question 6 tests the ladder: 14 days unanswered on 05/19/2027 sends a Notice of Delay to Lakeside's office manager that day, and 48 hours of silence moves it to Atty. Thorne on 05/21/2027.
summary.ask: Teresa Okafor calls and wants to talk about the gap. What do you say to her?

scale.say: Finally, the Skill Scale. Rate each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll compare your self-rating with your score, and where there's a big gap, we'll sit down and talk it through. And one last reminder: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive a value conversation with a carrier, no matter how well everything else went.
scale.ask: Which escalation skill from today do you most want to practice again before your next file?
